channel.title: Esubu Tech Academy blog
channel.description: Straight answers for Kenyan parents on kids coding, chess, screen time and school.

item.title: A phone for Christmas? What age to give one, and the settings to change on day one
item.description: A phone for Christmas? What a study of 100,000 young adults found about first-phone age, the kabambe route, and the settings to change on day one.

item.title: KJSEA results explained: what EE1 to BE2 mean, and what to do with each one
item.description: KJSEA slips show levels, not marks or a mean grade. What EE1 to BE2 mean subject by subject, and what to do with each result before Grade 10.

item.title: Your teenager and betting: the maths the odds don't show
item.description: 82.81% of young Kenyans surveyed had placed a bet. Teach your teenager the maths in the odds, the built-in margin, and a 1,000-bet test they run in Python.

item.title: Short videos and your child's focus: what 71 studies found, and how to rebuild attention
item.description: A review of 71 studies linked heavy short-video use with weaker attention. What it shows, what it doesn't, and a four-week focus ladder for home.

item.title: Grade 10 Computer Science in Kenya: what your child will learn, and how to prepare from Grade 7
item.description: KICD's Grade 10 Computer Science design gives 92 of 180 lessons to software development. What your child learns, and how to prepare from Grade 7.

item.title: Robotics or coding first? An honest answer for parents
item.description: Robotics looks more impressive than coding. What a robot needs before it moves, what kits cost you, and why coding first gives your child the robot's brain.

item.title: The first chess opening to teach your child: the Italian Game, move by move
item.description: Your child knows the moves and keeps losing in four. The Italian Game gives a plan for the first six moves, the reason for each, and a defence to the trap.

item.title: How a Kenyan child gets a FIDE rating, and what the number means
item.description: A first FIDE rating needs five games against rated players and starts at 1400 or higher. How the number is worked out, and the road for Kenyan children.

item.title: What comes after Scratch? The coding ladder from age 6 to 16
item.description: Scratch is the first rung. What comes next, from ScratchJr at five to Python, web pages and data science at sixteen, and what your child builds on each rung.

item.title: Computational thinking explained with ugali, matatus and laundry
item.description: Computational thinking sounds like jargon. It's four habits your child already uses at home: break problems down, spot patterns, drop details, write steps.

item.title: What your child builds in the first four weeks of coding and chess classes
item.description: We don't run trial classes, so here is the work instead: what your child learns in coding and chess, week by week, and what you see at home by week four.

item.title: Is holiday tuition illegal in Kenya? What the law says, and what your child does instead
item.description: Section 37 of the Basic Education Act bans holiday tuition, with fines up to KSh 100,000. What the 2025 Ministry memo says, and holiday options for your child.

item.title: Only 32 in 100 Grade 9 learners met the maths mark. How to help your child at home
item.description: Maths was the weakest KJSEA subject in 2025. What a study of 438 children found about parents and homework, and five daily habits for Kenyan homes.

item.title: Over 600,000 Grade 9 learners chose STEM. Is your child ready for it?
item.description: More than 600,000 KJSEA candidates chose STEM, yet only 32% met the maths mark. What the STEM pathway asks of your child, and what to build from Grade 4.

item.title: Should your child use ChatGPT for homework? What happened to 1,000 students who did
item.description: Students using plain ChatGPT scored 48% better in practice, then 17% worse in the exam once it was taken away. What the study means for your child's homework.

item.title: Free coding for kids in Kenya: what's out there, and where free runs out
item.description: Scratch, Code Clubs and free chess sites cost nothing but data. What each gives your child, where free runs out, and why we don't run free trial classes.

item.title: Chess tournaments for kids in Kenya: from the kitchen table to the nationals
item.description: 4,700 children aged 7 to 17 played Kenya's 2026 under-17 nationals. How junior chess tournaments work in Kenya, from clubs and qualifiers to the national stage.

item.title: Should your daughter learn to code? What Kenya's Grade 9 results suggest
item.description: Girls beat boys in 10 of 12 KJSEA subjects in 2025, yet women remain a small minority of Africa's developers. Where the gap opens, and what parents do about it.

item.title: Learning to code on a phone: what your child needs at home, and what they don't
item.description: Most Kenyan homes have a phone, few have a computer. What a phone, tablet and laptop each do for a child learning to code, and the data a Zoom class uses.

item.title: The jobs growing fastest by 2030, and what developers earn in Kenya
item.description: The World Economic Forum lists AI specialists and software developers among the fastest-growing jobs to 2030. What developers earn in Kenya.

item.title: 72 days at home: a December holiday plan for Nairobi kids
item.description: Kenyan schools closed on 23 October and reopen on 4 January 2027. A weekly holiday plan for Nairobi parents, with free and paid ideas for each morning.

item.title: Screen time for kids: what your child does on the screen counts more than the hours
item.description: Most Nairobi children pass two hours of screen time on weekends. What to count instead of hours, what to swap, and a ten-minute test to run tonight.

item.title: AI writes code now. Should your child still learn to code?
item.description: AI tools write code in seconds. Is coding still worth learning for children in Kenya? What studies of AI and programmers show, and a test to try.

item.title: Choosing a coding class for your child in Kenya: 9 questions to ask before you pay
item.description: Before you pay for a kids coding class in Kenya, ask these nine questions about the teacher, group size, recordings, your child's data and results.

item.title: Does chess make children smarter? What the research says
item.description: Chess is sold to parents as an IQ and maths booster. The largest studies say otherwise. What chess does do for children, and how to check it at home.

item.title: Your child cried after losing a chess game. Good.
item.description: When a child cries after losing a game, the first ten minutes matter most. What to say, what to skip, and how replaying the lost game turns it into a lesson.

item.title: How to teach your child chess at home in 7 days
item.description: A day-by-day plan to teach your child chess at home in 20 minutes a day, even if you play badly. Mini-games for each piece and a first full game.

item.title: What age should a child start coding? A straight answer for parents
item.description: No single right age exists for coding, but each age suits a different kind. An age-by-age guide for Kenyan parents and a five-minute readiness test.

item.title: Scratch or Python first? How to choose for your child
item.description: Scratch or Python first for your child? What a 15-week classroom study found, a simple rule based on typing and reading, and signs it's time to switch.

item.title: Coding in Kenyan schools: what the KICD-approved curriculum means for your child
item.description: Kenya approved a school coding curriculum in 2022. What the approval covers, what it leaves to parents, and five questions to ask your child's school.
